newsitem.title: USA: Union says hopes Bridgestone pact ends dispute.
newsitem.headline: Union says hopes Bridgestone pact ends dispute.

text.p: United Steelworkers union officials said Wednesday their tentative agreement with Bridgestone Corp. U.S. unit was a union victory that they hope will end their long and bitter dispute with the Japanese tiremaker.
Meanwhile, the U.S. unit, Bridgestone/Firestone Inc., said the strike and a related union boycott of the company's products have not hurt this year's sales and income.
The unit is on target to meet its previous forecast of $6 billion in sales and $180 million in income in 1996, spokesman Trevor Hoskins said.

"We are expected to have record sales this year and record income for Bridgestone/Firestone," Hoskins said. "Our sales have increased (and) our market share has increased in the last two years" despite the strike.

About 4,000 United Rubber Workers, now part of the Steelworkers union, struck five of the tiremaker's U.S. facilities in July, 1994, but the plants operated throughout the strike. The company, which hired replacement workers, has recalled most of the strikers, it said.

Hoskins said the union's boycott and "corporate campaign" against Bridgestone- and Firestone-brand products "did not work. Americans do not believe in boycotts. They just don't support them," he said.
In fact, he said, Bridgestone/Firestone is selling all the tires it can produce. It will make 41 million tires this year, up from 21 million five years ago, he said.
The tentative agreement covers more than 6,000 workers at four tire plants and three other facilities.
The company said it is "very satisfied" with the tentative pact and optimistic that union members will ratify it.
But the union said the dispute isn't over until it's over.

"There are still a lot of issues to be worked out," United Steelworkers president George Becker said at a news conference in Pittsburgh, where the union is based. "We hope this is the end of a long struggle with the company."

Union officials said the new agreement, reached early Monday after several days of round-the-clock negotiations, includes a 40-cent an hour wage increase and a signing bonus but said job security provisions were not addressed to the union's satisfaction.
